move: Quotes the National Assembly's declaration of natural, imprescriptible and inalienable rights and makes their preservation the stated end of all political association, against which legislative and executive acts are to be compared.
Defines natural rights as those belonging to man in right of his existence and grounds every civil right in a pre-existing natural right retained or pooled on entering society.

Argues that power aggregated from surrendered natural rights can never be turned against the natural rights individuals retain, then sorts governments by whether they arise from the common rights of man or from superstition and conquest.

Holds that legislative power aimed only at preservation can never acquire a right to destroy or enslave, since the law of nature binds legislators as an eternal rule and no human sanction is valid against it.
Defines natural liberty as being subject only to the law of nature, and liberty in society as living under a standing consented rule rather than another man's arbitrary will.

Presents the American and French revolutions as restoring a natural order and restates the articles making preservation of the natural and imprescriptible rights of man the end of political association.

Divides natural rights into those retained (where individual power suffices, such as the rights of the mind and religion) and those deposited in society, concluding that civil power is just aggregated natural right.

Claims that historically and in the order of nature the State precedes the individual, so rights are gradually acquired through social development rather than held by original ordinance of nature, leaving the individual with no rights against the social organism.
Argues that men entered society not to have fewer rights but to have them better secured, making natural rights the foundation of all civil rights.

Asserts that no society is free whatever its form of government unless these liberties are respected absolutely, while grounding the claim in the gains mankind reaps from letting each pursue his own good.
Argues from nature's unpredictable distribution of mental powers that hereditary government is repugnant to human rights as well as to human wisdom, and therefore unjust.

Argues that social order arises from the natural constitution of man and mutual dependence prior to government, limiting how much government man actually needs, without asserting rights government must respect.
